questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Rational Equations by Factoring a Quadratic Denominator With No Constant Term
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{6}{v+4}+\frac{12}{v(v+4)}=\frac{3}{v}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(v+4,\,v(v+4),\,v)=v(v+4).
$$

- The values $v=0$ and $v=-4$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{v+4}+\frac{12}{v(v+4)} & =\frac{3}{v} \\ v(v+4)\cdot (\frac{6}{v+4}+\frac{12}{v(v+4)}) & =v(v+4)\cdot \frac{3}{v} \\ \frac{6v(v+4)}{v+4}+\frac{12v(v+4)}{v(v+4)} & =\frac{3v(v+4)}{v} \\ \frac{6v\cdot \cancel{(v+4)}}{\cancel{v+4}}+\frac{12\cdot \cancel{v(v+4)}}{\cancel{v(v+4)}} & =\frac{3\cdot \cancel{v}\cdot (v+4)}{\cancel{v}} \\ 6v+12 & =3(v+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $v,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6v+12 & =3(v+4) \\ 6v+12 & =3v+12 \\ 3v & =0 \\ v & =0\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $v=0$  is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Rational Equations by Factoring a Quadratic Denominator With No Constant Term
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{1}{r(r-1)}-\frac{1}{r-1}=\frac{1}{3r}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(r(r-1),\,r-1,\,3r)=3r(r-1).
$$

- The values $r=0$ and $r=1$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{r(r-1)}-\frac{1}{r-1} & =\frac{1}{3r} \\ 3r(r-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{r(r-1)}-\frac{1}{r-1}) & =3r(r-1)\cdot \frac{1}{3r} \\ \frac{3r(r-1)}{r(r-1)}-\frac{3r(r-1)}{r-1} & =\frac{3r(r-1)}{3r} \\ \frac{3\cdot \cancel{r(r-1)}}{\cancel{r(r-1)}}-\frac{3r\cdot \cancel{(r-1)}}{\cancel{r-1}} & =\frac{\cancel{3r}\cdot (r-1)}{\cancel{3r}} \\ 3-3r & =r-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $r,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-3r & =r-1 \\ 4 & =4r \\ r & =1\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $r=1$ is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations by Factoring a Quadratic Trinomial
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{3}{R-1}-\frac{2}{R-2}=\frac{2}{(R-1)(R-2)}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(R-1,\,R-2,\,(R-1)(R-2))=(R-1)(R-2).
$$

- The values $R=1$ and $R=2$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{R-1}-\frac{2}{R-2} & =\frac{2}{(R-1)(R-2)} \\ (R-1)(R-2)\cdot (\frac{3}{R-1}-\frac{2}{R-2}) & =(R-1)(R-2)\cdot \frac{2}{(R-1)(R-2)} \\ \frac{3(R-1)(R-2)}{R-1}-\frac{2(R-1)(R-2)}{R-2} & =\frac{2(R-1)(R-2)}{(R-1)(R-2)} \\ \frac{\cancel{(R-1)}\cdot 3(R-2)}{\cancel{R-1}}-\frac{2(R-1)\cdot \cancel{(R-2)}}{\cancel{R-2}} & =\frac{2\cdot \cancel{(R-1)(R-2)}}{\cancel{(R-1)(R-2)}} \\ 3(R-2)-2(R-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving this equation for $R,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(R-2)-2(R-1) & =2 \\ 3R-6-2R+2 & =2 \\ R & =6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $6\ne 1$ and $6\ne 2,$ we conclude that $R=6$ is a valid solution. 

Therefore, the solution to our original equation is $R=6.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations by Factoring a Quadratic Trinomial
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{1}{a-3}-\frac{10}{(a+1)(a-3)}=\frac{2}{a+1}
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(a+1,\,a-3,\,(a+1)(a-3))=(a+1)(a-3).
$$

- The values $a=-1$ and $a=3$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{a-3}-\frac{10}{(a+1)(a-3)} & =\frac{2}{a+1} \\ (a+1)(a-3)\cdot (\frac{1}{a-3}-\frac{10}{(a+1)(a-3)}) & =(a+1)(a-3)\cdot \frac{2}{a+1} \\ \frac{(a+1)(a-3)}{a-3}-\frac{10(a+1)(a-3)}{(a+1)(a-3)} & =\frac{2(a+1)(a-3)}{a+1} \\ \frac{(a+1)\cdot \cancel{(a-3)}}{\cancel{a-3}}-\frac{10\cdot \cancel{(a+1)(a-3)}}{\cancel{(a+1)(a-3)}} & =\frac{2\cdot \cancel{(a+1)}\cdot (a-3)}{\cancel{a+1}} \\ a+1-10 & =2(a-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $a,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}a+1-10 & =2(a-3) \\ a-9 & =2a-6 \\ a & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-3\ne -1$ and $-3\ne 3,$ we conclude that $a=-3$ is a valid solution. 

Therefore, the solution to our original equation is $a=-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Rational Equations by Factoring a Quadratic Denominator With No Constant Term
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{7}{h}-\frac{3}{2h-3}=\frac{1}{h(2h-3)}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(h,\,2h-3,\,h(2h-3))=h(2h-3).
$$

- The values $h=0$ and $h=\frac{3}{2}$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{h}-\frac{3}{2h-3} & =\frac{1}{h(2h-3)} \\ h(2h-3)\cdot (\frac{7}{h}-\frac{3}{2h-3}) & =h(2h-3)\cdot \frac{1}{h(2h-3)} \\ \frac{7h(2h-3)}{h}-\frac{3h(2h-3)}{2h-3} & =\frac{h(2h-3)}{h(2h-3)} \\ \frac{7\cdot \cancel{h}(2h-3)}{\cancel{h}}-\frac{3h\cdot \cancel{(2h-3)}}{\cancel{2h-3}} & =\frac{\cancel{h(2h-3)}}{\cancel{h(2h-3)}} \\ 7(2h-3)-3h & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $h,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}7(2h-3)-3h & =1 \\ 14h-21-3h & =1 \\ 11h & =22 \\ h & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2\ne 0$ and $2\ne \frac{3}{2},$ we conclude that $h=2$ is a valid solution. 

Therefore, the solution to our original equation is $h=2.$
